source_file: zhihu_应聘时何时适合谈薪资.txt

heuristics.rule: State your expected salary as a specific number, not a range or deflection
heuristics.condition: When HR asks for your salary expectation during the offer negotiation stage...
heuristics.action: Give a direct, specific number (e.g., 'I am looking for X per year') rather than deflecting, asking them to name a price first, or saying you have no requirements
heuristics.because: Multiple HR commenters across the thread independently stated they prefer candidates who give direct numbers — it signals self-awareness and saves negotiation time. Deflecting forces HR into an awkward position since they cannot quote a final number without knowing candidate expectations first.

heuristics.rule: Add ~10% buffer on top of your true expected salary when stating it to HR
heuristics.condition: When you have determined your market value and are about to state your expected salary...
heuristics.action: Quote a number approximately 10% above your actual floor so there is room for HR to 'negotiate down' while you still land at an acceptable number
heuristics.because: Multiple commenters from the job-seeker perspective noted this as standard practice — if the company wants you, they will negotiate and you will land closer to your real target; if they don't, they will contact you to discuss.

heuristics.rule: Research salary benchmarks across at least three channels before entering any negotiation
heuristics.condition: Before any salary discussion with HR...
heuristics.action: Check job listing salary ranges on platforms like 拉勾/猎聘, consult a headhunter in your domain, and if possible tap senior industry contacts — then take the median as your market value baseline
heuristics.because: Both the HR and the job-seeker commenter independently described this triangulation approach as the foundation for credible negotiation; without it, candidates either undershoot or make unrealistic demands.

heuristics.rule: A 20–30% salary increase is the standard jump expectation when changing jobs
heuristics.condition: When calculating your target salary for a job change...
heuristics.action: Use your current total compensation as the base and target 20–30% above it as your asking price
heuristics.because: The headhunter commenter stated this explicitly as '跳槽行规' (industry norm for job-hopping); the HR commenter also cited 10–20% as a normal range, with strong performers able to push higher.

heuristics.rule: Do not raise salary questions during technical interviews or phone screens — wait for the HR interview
heuristics.condition: When you want to ask about salary range or compensation structure...
heuristics.action: Hold all salary questions until you are in a formal HR interview, not during phone screens or hiring-manager rounds
heuristics.because: The headhunter commenter explicitly listed this as a key negotiation rule — asking prematurely signals poor judgment and may undermine your position before the company has fully evaluated you.

heuristics.rule: If an offer comes in below 80% of your expected salary or below your current salary, decline without extended negotiation
heuristics.condition: When you receive an offer that is significantly below your expectation...
heuristics.action: Politely decline rather than continuing to negotiate, unless there is exceptional non-monetary value
heuristics.because: The job-seeker commenter noted that departments have fixed salary bands and pushing for 20–30% above their number is unrealistic; continuing wastes both parties' time.

decision_factors.factor: Whether HR raises salary at the very start of the process
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Early salary discussion signals low flexibility — the role has a fixed band with little or no negotiation room, and HR is using it as a filter criterion rather than a negotiation starting point
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Note at what stage HR first brings up compensation. If it's in the initial phone screen, the band is likely rigid.

decision_factors.factor: Degree of hiring manager enthusiasm (as relayed by HR)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: When the hiring team is 'very satisfied' vs 'satisfied' vs 'acceptable', the salary ceiling HR is authorized to offer differs significantly — very satisfied candidates may have no cap imposed
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Pay attention to HR's tone and urgency when they call back. How quickly they move to close, and whether they initiate salary discussion proactively, signals enthusiasm level.

decision_factors.factor: Whether you hold competing offers at similar level companies
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Competing offers give HR a concrete justification to bring to the hiring team to push for a higher salary — without this, HR's internal advocacy has no anchor
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Actively collect multiple offers before negotiating; the job-seeker commenter and the headhunter both cite this as a direct lever.

decision_factors.factor: Internal salary equity constraints at the target company
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Even if HR wants to give you more, team-wide salary bands prevent it — HR cannot break internal equity without disrupting the whole team
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask during the HR interview how salary adjustments are structured, and whether the role has a defined band. Companies that cannot clearly explain their compensation structure are a red flag.

decision_factors.factor: Job market timing (hiring season vs. off-season)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: More open roles in Q1-Q2 (金三银四) means higher candidate leverage; fewer roles in Q4 means lower leverage
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Align active job searching and negotiation to peak hiring periods (March–April) when possible; avoid year-end transitions that also sacrifice annual bonuses.

decision_factors.factor: Your current salary as a baseline anchor
decision_factors.why_it_matters: HR uses your current compensation as a reference point when advocating internally for your package — but it is a reference, not a ceiling
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Disclose accurately (background checks and pay stubs verify it), but frame it alongside your demonstrated value and target growth trajectory.

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Underquoting your salary expectation to seem more hireable
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You anchor all future raises, bonuses, and pension contributions to a lower base — the cumulative loss over time far exceeds the short-term hiring advantage
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career professionals (2–5 years experience) who are optimizing for getting the offer rather than long-term earnings

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Declining to disclose your expected salary and asking HR to name a number first
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: HR cannot quote a final number before knowing your expectations — so this tactic forces HR to either stall the process or make an uninformed internal recommendation, reducing the chance of a good outcome for you
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who have read negotiation advice telling them 'never show your cards first' and apply it rigidly

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a platform/brand name company at a salary discount
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You lose the income immediately, and the 'prestige value' only materializes if future employers actually value that brand — which is not guaranteed in all industries
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early-to-mid career professionals who prioritize resume signaling over current compensation

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving a job in Q4 to start a new one before annual bonus payout
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You forfeit that year's annual bonus — which can represent 1–3 months of additional income — for no gain
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Anyone considering a job change in October–December who has not accounted for bonus timing

failure_patterns.pattern: Refusing to state a salary expectation and asking HR to make the first offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates have absorbed the negotiation advice 'never reveal your bottom line first' and apply it in a context where it actively backfires — the HR-candidate dynamic is not a symmetric negotiation
failure_patterns.consequence: HR is put in an impossible position; they cannot finalize a number without candidate input, so the process stalls or HR makes a low internal recommendation to hedge the uncertainty
warning_signs: Candidate says 'whatever your standard is, just tell me'
Candidate says 'I have no salary requirements, I care more about the platform'

failure_patterns.pattern: Fabricating or inflating current salary figures
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates believe HR has no way to verify the number and use it to create a higher anchor for negotiation
failure_patterns.consequence: Background checks, bank statement requests, and payslip verification expose the lie — offer is rescinded at the final stage, which is a complete waste of both parties' time
warning_signs: Candidate hesitates or gives vague answers when asked for salary breakdown details
Stated salary is unusually high relative to experience level and market data

failure_patterns.pattern: Conflating the recruiter's question about salary expectation with the final offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates don't understand that when HR asks for expected salary early in the process, it is often intelligence gathering — not a binding negotiation — and panic-anchor to a low number
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidate inadvertently sets a low ceiling before the hiring team has fully evaluated them, leaving money on the table
warning_signs: Candidate quotes a number in early phone screen without being asked to negotiate
Candidate lowers their expectation preemptively 'to seem reasonable'

failure_patterns.pattern: Applying generic negotiation tactics (e.g., 'never show your cards') without understanding the HR-candidate structural dynamic
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Advice from negotiation books or online posts is context-free and does not account for the fact that HR must mediate between candidate and hiring team — they need candidate input to advocate effectively
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidate comes across as evasive or strategically naive; HR cannot build a case internally, reducing the chance of getting the full salary authorized
warning_signs: Candidate reflexively deflects every salary question
Candidate treats the HR interview as adversarial rather than collaborative

diagnostic_questions.question: At what point in the process did HR first raise salary — initial phone screen, or after technical interviews?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: If salary came up in the initial screen, the role likely has a fixed, non-negotiable band being used as a filter. If it came up after technical rounds, there is more likely genuine flexibility.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If early: ask HR directly whether the band is fixed. If yes, decide quickly whether you can accept it rather than wasting time in a full interview loop.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If after technical rounds: the hiring team has already evaluated you favorably — you have leverage. State your expectation confidently.

diagnostic_questions.question: Did HR ask for your salary expectation and then go quiet, or did they immediately start negotiating?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Going quiet means the hiring team has not yet finalized whether they want you — HR is gathering data before making an internal recommendation. Immediately negotiating means the team is ready to close.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they went quiet: don't follow up aggressively. Wait for their response — the decision is being made internally.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they started negotiating immediately: you are in the final stage. Be clear and firm about your number.

diagnostic_questions.question: Can you clearly articulate the full breakdown of your current compensation (base, bonus, equity, benefits)?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: If you cannot, you are not prepared for a professional salary conversation — HR will ask for this level of detail, and vagueness signals either dishonesty or lack of self-awareness.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: be ready to share it accurately, since background checks will verify it.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: gather your payslips, equity vesting schedules, and bonus records before entering any negotiation.

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a concrete sense of your market value from at least two independent data sources?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Without market data, any number you quote is a guess — and guesses tend to be either too low (leaving money on the table) or too high (ending negotiations prematurely).
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: you can state your expectation with confidence and justify it if challenged.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: do market research first — job boards, headhunters, or industry contacts — before entering the negotiation.

industry_realities.common_belief: Keeping your current salary secret gives you more negotiating power
industry_realities.actual_reality: Multiple HR commenters stated that current salary disclosure is standard practice, verified through background checks and payslip requests at offer stage — fabricating or withholding it only damages trust and can cause offer rescission
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should disclose current salary accurately, but shift the conversation toward future value and market benchmarks rather than anchoring solely on the current number

industry_realities.common_belief: HR is the adversary in salary negotiation — their job is to pay you as little as possible
industry_realities.actual_reality: HR commenters across the thread explained that HR's actual goal is to find a match point between candidate expectations and hiring team budget — they are intermediaries, not opponents, and a candidate who makes their job easy (clear expectations, honest data) gets better advocacy
industry_realities.implication: Treating HR as a collaborator and communicating clearly about your expectations improves your outcome more than treating them adversarially

industry_realities.common_belief: Once HR quotes a number, you can negotiate it up significantly
industry_realities.actual_reality: The HR commenter Hannah Han explicitly stated that once HR outputs a formal offer number, it is extremely difficult to revise — the internal approval process treats it as final
industry_realities.implication: Candidates must state their expectations clearly before HR formalizes the offer; post-offer negotiation has very limited upside

industry_realities.common_belief: Your previous salary caps what a new company will offer you
industry_realities.actual_reality: The HR commenter described a case where a candidate with a 5k current salary successfully negotiated a 15k offer based purely on demonstrated ability — multiple commenters agreed that ability, not prior salary, is the real ceiling
industry_realities.implication: Candidates with strong skills should not self-censor their expectations based on prior salary; the anchor that matters is market rate and demonstrated value, not history

industry_realities.common_belief: Entry-level and fresh graduates should not negotiate salary
industry_realities.actual_reality: The job-seeker commenter acknowledged that new graduates have low bargaining power in most cases, but attributed this to limited unique value rather than a rule against negotiating — exceptional candidates at any level can and should negotiate
industry_realities.implication: The real question is not 'should I negotiate' but 'do I have unique value that justifies negotiating' — focus on building that value rather than accepting the first number by default

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Response to 'what is your salary expectation?'
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Deflects, asks HR to name a number first, or says 'I have no requirements, I care about the platform' — trying to avoid anchoring too low while actually signaling lack of self-awareness
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: States a specific number confidently, justified by market research and a clear self-assessment of skills and value
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: HR explicitly prefers the direct answer — it signals self-awareness and enables HR to advocate effectively internally; deflection signals weakness and creates process friction

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Walks into the salary conversation with no market data, relying on gut feel or what a friend told them
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Has already triangulated market rate from job boards, headhunter input, and industry contacts; has a specific number and a justified rationale ready
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Without market data, any number quoted can be challenged or dismissed; with data, the candidate can hold their position credibly

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Understanding of what HR can and cannot do
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Believes HR decides salary and uses tactics to pressure HR directly into giving more
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Understands HR is a go-between who needs to justify the number to the hiring team — and therefore helps HR by providing clear, honest, specific information that makes the internal case easier
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Working with HR's structural constraints rather than against them produces better advocacy from HR and better outcomes

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Either accepts immediately to avoid seeming difficult, or argues emotionally without a structured counter
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Evaluates total compensation holistically (base + bonus + equity + benefits + career trajectory), states a specific counter based on market data, and is willing to walk away if the gap is too large
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Accepting too easily sacrifices long-term earnings; arguing without structure comes across as unprofessional — the data-backed counter is the only move that can actually change the outcome

community_misconceptions.misconception: Never show your bottom line — keep HR guessing to maximize your offer
community_misconceptions.why_believed: This advice comes from general negotiation theory where information asymmetry favors the side that reveals less
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: In hiring, HR cannot finalize or advocate for a salary internally without knowing candidate expectations — withholding this information stalls the process and reduces HR's ability to push for a higher number on your behalf
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: HR makes a conservative internal recommendation to hedge uncertainty, or the process stalls — in both cases the candidate ends up with a worse outcome than if they had stated their number clearly

community_misconceptions.misconception: Asking HR 'what do you think I'm worth?' is a clever tactic to get them to anchor high
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Candidates think this flatters HR into volunteering a high number, or at minimum avoids the candidate anchoring too low
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: HR commenters explicitly identified this as one of the most frustrating and counterproductive responses — HR cannot answer this question without a formal evaluation process, and the question signals that the candidate lacks self-awareness
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: HR forms a negative impression of the candidate's self-knowledge, which may reduce internal advocacy even if the technical interview went well

community_misconceptions.misconception: If you underquote to get the job, you'll make it up in later raises and bonuses
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The HR commenter Hannah Han partially endorsed this view — saying hard workers will eventually be rewarded regardless of starting salary
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: While the HR commenter stated this reassuringly, the structural reality (acknowledged elsewhere in the thread) is that raises are anchored to current salary, pension contributions are calculated on base pay, and 'making it up later' requires both a good company culture and continued outperformance — none of which are guaranteed
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates who accept below-market starting salaries often find the gap persists or widens; the reassurance that 'you'll be compensated later' is a risk transfer from employer to employee

real_case_outcomes.situation: A candidate with 2 years of experience and a current salary of 5,000 CNY/month applied for an e-commerce operations role and stated an expected salary of 15,000 CNY/month — a 3x ask
real_case_outcomes.decision: The HR interviewer and hiring manager decided to interview him despite the unusual gap; he spent 2 hours demonstrating concrete operational value
real_case_outcomes.outcome: The hiring manager circled the 15,000 figure on his form and told HR to offer exactly that — the prior 5k salary became completely irrelevant
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Exceptional demonstrated ability overrides prior salary as an anchor entirely; the risk of quoting a high number is only that you don't get the interview — once you're in the room, your value is what determines the offer

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate refuses to state a salary number and says 'I care more about the platform and growth opportunities than salary'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Fear of anchoring too low combined with imposter syndrome — the candidate lacks confidence in their market value and uses platform-framing as a face-saving deflection
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: The candidate avoids any salary commitment, hoping the company will surprise them with a good offer — but comes across as either dishonest or lacking self-awareness to experienced HR
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe the task: 'What is your market rate?' is not a trap — it is an invitation to advocate for yourself. Preparing a specific number backed by market data turns a fear-based deflection into a confident, informed answer.

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate asks whether they should disclose their current (low) salary given that their expectation is much higher
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Shame about current compensation level combined with fear that disclosure will cap the offer — the candidate treats past salary as a verdict on their worth rather than a starting point
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate either lies about current salary or refuses to disclose it, creating verification risk and signaling untrustworthiness
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Disclose accurately and immediately shift the frame: 'My current salary is X, and based on my market research and the value I can bring to this role, I'm targeting Y.' This separates the factual anchor from the aspirational one.

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate accepts a below-expectation offer immediately without counter-offering, citing fear of seeming difficult or losing the offer
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Scarcity mindset — treating any offer as a gift that could be taken away, rather than as a mutual transaction where both parties have leverage
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate says yes immediately or says 'I'll take whatever you can offer' — leaving money on the table and often feeling resentful afterward
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Remind the candidate: HR has already decided to make an offer, which means they want you. The negotiation at this point is low-risk — a reasonable counter rarely causes an offer to be rescinded. State the counter once, clearly, with a rationale.

reframing_moves.original_framing: How do I strategically avoid revealing my salary expectations so HR can't lowball me?
reframing_moves.reframe: HR cannot advocate for you internally without knowing your expectations — withholding this information doesn't protect you, it handicaps the person trying to get you more money
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the candidate from an adversarial frame (HR vs. me) to a structural one (HR as intermediary who needs my input) — changes the optimal behavior from concealment to clear communication
reframing_moves.example_language: HR在完全不了解候选人期望的前提下就和用人部门确定了薪酬，如果那个数字与候选人预期有较大差距，这次录用就只能以失败收尾了

reframing_moves.original_framing: My current salary is low — if I reveal it, they'll only offer me a small increase
reframing_moves.reframe: Your current salary is a reference point, not a ceiling — what actually determines your offer is demonstrated ability and market rate, and these can be completely disconnected from your history
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Breaks the cognitive link between past salary and future offer, freeing the candidate to negotiate based on value rather than defending a prior anchor
reframing_moves.example_language: 之前的5k变得没有任何意义，也没有任何人再去关注这个数字

reframing_moves.original_framing: I should ask HR what they think I'm worth, so I don't anchor too low
reframing_moves.reframe: Asking HR to value you signals that you don't know your own value — the person who should know what you're worth is you, because you're the seller and sellers set the asking price
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Uses the buyer-seller market analogy to make it intuitive why the candidate (seller) should name the price first — removes the feeling that stating a number first is a weakness
reframing_moves.example_language: 在一对一的谈判过程中，最有效率也最合理的方式一定是卖方先出价，因为卖方最清楚自己的能力和价值
